records.answer: You can connect Cursor to Ark by adding the Ark MCP server to Cursor. The MCP config should be placed in `.cursor/mcp.json`, either globally at `~/.cursor/mcp.json` or project-scoped at the repo root. The config should have the shape `{ "mcpServers": { "ark": { "type": "http", "url": "https://ark.internal.ap-south-1.platform.mlops.pai.mypaytm.com/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer <YOUR_KEY>" } } } }`, where `<YOUR_KEY>` is your user key. You can also add it through Cursor's settings by finding the MCP servers list and adding an HTTP server named `ark` with the URL ending in `/mcp` and the `Authorization: Bearer <YOUR_KEY>` header.

Cursor shows up in Foundry in two unrelated ways, and this page covers both.
The first is Cursor as your editor: it connects to the control plane's MCP server and gets the `ark` toolbox, so you can dispatch sessions, inspect flows and steer runs without leaving Cursor. The second is Cursor as a **runtime** , one of the harnesses Foundry dispatches agents onto, alongside the `claude-agent` and `pi-dev` families and their `-pi-inference` gateway variants. In that mode nobody is sitting in the editor at all: a stage runs on Cursor's agent SDK, on an EC2 box, a registered host or in a Kubernetes pod, and reports back like any other stage.

records.answer: You can set up your own EC2 box as compute by having Foundry install `arkd` on it over SSM. The exact command to run on the box itself is not specified, but Foundry can install `arkd` on it. To set capacity on the box, you can use the command `ark compute update <your-machine> --set capacity`. Additionally, you'll need to adopt the box, not enroll it, as enrolling only registers the box and doesn't give it capacity.

An `ec2` compute is usually a machine Foundry owns end to end: it launches the instance in your AWS account, installs `arkd` on it over SSM, stops it when it goes idle, and terminates it when you destroy the row. The same kind can also adopt a box you already run, in which case Foundry installs `arkd` and nothing else, as below. That is the difference from [registering a machine you already own](/onboarding/registering-compute), where the box dials in and Foundry never touches its lifecycle.
You create it in one of two shapes. A **dedicated box** is a single named instance your team's sessions land on, which is what most teams start with. ## Team-scoped secrets 
Teams can override identity secrets (Bitbucket bot user, own `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`, JFrog account) for all their members at once - web UI → Secrets → Add secret → scope **team**.
Resolution is **user → team → tenant** , first hit per key wins; a team that sets nothing simply inherits tenant defaults. Team writes require a team-admin grant for that team (or tenant-admin).
WARNING
Never override infra values (`JIRA_BASE_URL`, JFrog URL, etc.) at team scope - it becomes invisible per-team configuration drift that looks like "Ark is broken only for our team."

## Adding a user to the tenant 
Account creation (Cognito login + tenant membership) is done by the platform team - send the email and team name (or a .csv for a whole team) to a tenant admin, listed on the **Settings** page under **Your admins**. Once the user exists, you control _what they can do_ with grants:
bash
    
    ark grant <email> --role member                       # tenant-wide member (default scope: tenant)
    ark grant <email> --role team-admin --scope team:<team-slug>
    ark grant list <email>                                # see someone's live grants
    ark grant revoke <grant-id>                           # remove one
Roles: `tenant-admin` | `team-admin` | `member` | `viewer`. Grants are the authority primitive - a team grant covers that team's subtree.

records.answer: You can link your Slack identity to your Ark identity either through the web UI by clicking Generate on the Connect Slack card, or via CLI using `ark slack link` with your API key. After minting your link token, DM it to the Ark bot in Slack to confirm the link. Alternatively, you can use the one-click Connect Slack card on the Onboarding page, which needs neither the CLI nor an API key. If you choose the CLI way, run `ark slack link` with your personal API key, then DM the token to the bot within 15 minutes. Do not use the `--force` flag, as it is a tenant-admin action that fails on your own account with a permission denied error.

records.answer: Devops needs to set up an EKS cluster, configure the AWS CLI for the account the cluster is in, and point kubectl at that cluster. They also need to create a namespace for the conductor, as 'self' needs no setup beyond a namespace. Additionally, they may need to unlock the tenant to target the specific k8s cluster, as a tenant can be locked to specific clusters. If the cluster is not in the same account as the control plane, they need to provide the 'roleArn' and 'externalId' for cross-account access. Once the cluster is set up, they can create a k8s pool using the 'compute' MCP tool or the 'compute/pool/create' JSON-RPC endpoint.

A `k8s` compute is not a machine. It is a pool row holding the cluster, the namespace, the pod image and the pod's resource limits, and every dispatch cuts one pod from it for one session. # Bring your own agents and flows 
Once you have run a session with a built-in flow, you can register your own. This page is for that point, not for your first day: it assumes you are comfortable dispatching a session and now want your team's own process encoded.
If you have not run a session yet, go to [Run your first session](/onboarding/getting-started) first. Nothing here is needed to get started.

## Register your own 
Do this from a terminal where `ark` is on your PATH. All three commands read from a YAML file.
**Step 1 - Define your agents.** Write each agent as a YAML file. Two keys are required: `name` (kebab-case) and `runtime` (a worker needs one to be dispatchable -- there is no default, and dispatch hard-fails without it). Everything else has a default, but you will normally also set `model`, `system_prompt`, and `tools`. Note the scope: agents register **project-scoped** by default while flows register **global** by default (Step 3), so a global flow cannot see a project-scoped agent at dispatch -- the `--global` below keeps them in the same scope. Register each one:
bash
    
    ark agent create myteam-reviewer --from myteam-reviewer.yaml --no-editor --global
    ark agent list          # confirm it shows up

yaml
    
    name

You can link your Slack identity to your Ark identity either from the web UI or from the CLI.

**Web UI (quickest)**
1. Open the **Onboarding** tab in the Ark web UI.
2. Click **Generate** on the **Connect Slack** card – this mints a link token for you.
3. Open a direct‑message conversation with the Ark bot in Slack and paste the token you just received.
4. The bot will confirm that your accounts are linked and you can start using `/ark` commands.

**CLI method**
1. Make sure you have a personal, identity‑bound API key (not a shared key).
2. In any terminal run:
   `ark slack link \
      --server https://ark.internal.ap-south-1.platform.ml-pays.com \
      --token <YOUR_ARK_API_KEY>`
   (replace the server URL and your API key as needed). The command prints a token that is valid for 15 minutes.
3. Immediately open a direct‑message with the Ark bot in Slack and send the token (or run `ark link <token>` in the DM).
4. After the bot confirms the link, you can run `/ark` in any channel where the bot is invited and Ark will dispatch sessions as you.

**Tips**
- Do **not** add the `--force` flag; it is a tenant‑admin action and will give a “permission denied: tenant.admin at tenant scope” error.
- If the token expires or the DM does not reach the bot, repeat steps 2‑3.
- If you cannot DM the bot, give your Slack member ID to a tenant admin for them to link you manually.

records.answer: Your DevOps team needs to prepare the cluster before you can dispatch to a k8s pool. First, create a namespace in the target cluster – a “self” cluster needs only that namespace because the conductor is already running there. Then make sure the cluster is reachable from the control plane: configure the AWS CLI for the account that owns the cluster, set `kubectl` to point at the cluster, and sign in the `ark` CLI to your control plane. If the cluster lives in a different AWS account, add the cross‑account credentials (`roleArn` and `externalId`) to the pool definition; omit them when the cluster is in the same account. Finally, verify that the tenant is permitted to target the chosen k8s cluster (a locked tenant will cause a “Tenant … is not permitted …” error). Once those prerequisites are in place you can create the k8s pool and dispatch sessions to it.

You can register either device – the steps are just a little different.

**MacBook (macOS)**
* If you don’t have sudo you can install the runtime (bun) yourself and enroll as your own user:
  1. Install bun (if needed): `curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash`.
  2. Enroll the box with a launch‑agent that runs under your login: `ark host enroll <name> --isolation direct --launchd`.
  3. Verify with `ark --version` and `ark host status <name>` and then you can dispatch a session to it.
  (This flow is described in chunks 8 and 9.)
* If you have sudo you can also use the one‑command script which will set up a systemd unit (on Linux) or a launch‑agent (on macOS) for you. Run the script as root or as the user that should own the enrollment, providing `API_KEY` and `MACHINE_NAME` (e.g. `API_KEY=ark_t-... MACHINE_NAME=my‑mac ./ark-enroll-host.sh`). (See chunks 3‑7.)

**EC2 box (Linux)**
* Use the same one‑command enrollment script on the instance:
  1. `curl -fsSL https://foundry.mypaytm.com/ark-enroll-host.sh -o ark-enroll-host.sh && chmod +x ark-enroll-host.sh`
  2. `API_KEY=ark_t-... MACHINE_NAME=my‑ec2 ./ark-enroll-host.sh`
  3. The script installs the CLI, logs in, enrolls `arkd` on port 19300, creates a systemd unit, and sets capacity based on the VM’s hardware.
  4. Re‑running the script is safe – it will stop the existing `arkd`, rotate the token, and refresh everything.
  (See chunks 3‑7 for the script details and chunk 10 for the manual equivalent `ark host enroll … --systemd`.)

So you can register your MacBook directly with `ark host enroll … --launchd` (or the script) or ask for an EC2 box and run the same script there with `--systemd`. Both are supported; choose the machine that best fits where you want to run sessions.

# Bring your own agents and flows 
Once you have run a session with a built-in flow, you can register your own. This page is for that point, not for your first day: it assumes you are comfortable dispatching a session and now want your team's own process encoded.
If you have not run a session yet, go to [Run your first session](/onboarding/getting-started) first. Nothing here is needed to get started.

## Register your own 
Do this from a terminal where `ark` is on your PATH. All three commands read from a YAML file.
**Step 1 - Define your agents.** Write each agent as a YAML file. Two keys are required: `name` (kebab-case) and `runtime` (a worker needs one to be dispatchable -- there is no default, and dispatch hard-fails without it). Everything else has a default, but you will normally also set `model`, `system_prompt`, and `tools`. Note the scope: agents register **project-scoped** by default while flows register **global** by default (Step 3), so a global flow cannot see a project-scoped agent at dispatch -- the `--global` below keeps them in the same scope. Register each one:
bash
    
    ark agent create myteam-reviewer --from myteam-reviewer.yaml --no-editor --global
    ark agent list          # confirm it shows up

yaml

## 3\. Set up a workspace 
A workspace is your project written down once: which repos to clone, which tools to install, which services to run, and which secrets a session needs. It is rebuilt fresh for every session, so an agent starts with a working checkout and a ready toolchain instead of guessing how to build your project.

### 0. Make Ark Reliable

**Goal:** Stop the outages before we add anything new.

- Stop 503s: credential-refresh grant for the weekly DB password rotation, plus event-consumer backpressure.
- Redis recovery, and managed EC2 or EKS instead of laptops.
- Team-scoped compute and credentials, with pre-flight prerequisite checks.
- Prevent an arkd disconnect from stranding a run; detect machine loss and recover.
- Do not kill a healthy long build, and surface no silent hangs.
- Pause and resume on a rate limit, and preserve work on every kill.
- Reduce UI polling, keep auth stable under load, and deliver Slack alarms.

You can link your Slack identity to Ark in two ways:

**CLI method**
1. Make sure you have a personal, identity‑bound API key (the one you got from the Getting Access page).
2. In any terminal run the link command (do **not** add `--force`):
```
ark slack link \
  --server https://ark.internal.ap-south-1.platform.mlops.pai.mypaytm.com \
  --token <YOUR_ARK_API_KEY>
```
   The command prints a one‑time token that is valid for 15 minutes.
3. Open a direct message with the Ark bot in Slack and run:
```
ark link <token‑from‑step‑2>
```
   The bot will confirm that your accounts are linked.

**Web UI (quick) method**
1. Open the **Onboarding** tab in the Ark web UI.
2. Click **Generate** on the **Connect Slack** card – this mints the same one‑time token without needing the CLI or an API key.
3. DM the token (or run `ark link <token>`) to the Ark bot in Slack.
4. The bot confirms the link.

After the link is confirmed you can use `/ark` commands in any channel where the bot is present and Ark will DM you for session updates and approvals. If you see “Your Slack account is not linked”, redo steps 2‑3 because the token may have expired or the DM didn’t arrive.

Your DevOps team needs to prepare the target Kubernetes cluster before you can dispatch to a k8s pool. They must:
1. Create a namespace in the cluster (the only requirement for a `"self"` pool because the conductor is already running there). 
2. Make sure the tenant is allowed to target that cluster – if the tenant is locked to specific clusters, pool creation will fail with a permission error. 
3. Have an `ark` CLI that is signed in to your control‑plane, an AWS CLI configured for the account that owns the cluster, and `kubectl` pointed at the cluster. 
With those pieces in place you can create the pool (using the compute MCP tool) and dispatch sessions to it.

You can register either your MacBook or an EC2 Linux instance – the enrollment process differs only by the init system the host uses.

**MacBook (macOS)**
1. Install the prerequisites if they aren’t already present, e.g. `bun` (``curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash``).  
2. Enroll the box with a launch‑agent that runs under your login user: ``ark host enroll <NAME> --isolation direct --launchd``.  
   *The `--launchd` flag creates a LaunchAgent that starts `arkd` at login, so the daemon survives reboots without needing sudo.*
3. Verify the install with ``ark --version`` and ``ark host status <NAME>``.
4. (Optional) Use the one‑command script instead of manual steps: set `API_KEY` and `MACHINE_NAME` then run ``./ark-enroll-host.sh`` – it will install the CLI, install `bun` and Claude Code if missing, enroll the host, and register a systemd unit (or LaunchAgent on macOS).

**EC2 (Linux)**
1. Ensure the machine can reach the control plane on port 443.
2. Enroll the box with a systemd service so it starts at boot: ``ark host enroll <NAME> --isolation direct --systemd`` (run as root or with passwordless sudo).  
   *The `--systemd` flag writes a systemd unit that starts `arkd` on boot, keeping the worker alive across reboots.*
3. Verify with ``ark --version`` and ``ark host status <NAME>``.
4. As with macOS, you can use the one‑command script: provide ``API_KEY`` and ``MACHINE_NAME`` then run ``./ark-enroll-host.sh`` to perform the same steps automatically.

Both platforms are supported; choose the one that matches the hardware you want to use.

You’re hitting the same thing that shows up in the Ark repo‑access docs. In Ark the push that creates a PR must be done with the SSH key that lives in Ark Secrets, not just a local PAT.

1. **Generate a passphrase‑free SSH private key** and add the public key to the Bitbucket workspace that owns the repo.
2. **Store the private key in an Ark secret** named `BITBUCKET_SSH_KEY_<WORKSPACE>` where `<WORKSPACE>` exactly matches the Bitbucket workspace name (e.g. `BITBUCKET_SSH_KEY_PAYTMTEAM`). The suffix matters – using the wrong secret makes the key look unauthorized.
3. **Verify the key works** from your own machine before running through Ark: `ssh -i ~/.ssh/ark_bitbucket -T git@bitbucket.org` (you should see a welcome message, not a permission‑denied error).
4. **Make sure the secret is attached to your Ark tenant** (right tenant, secrets added) and that your workspace YAML references it if a workspace needs it.
5. **Do not rely on a personal access token for pushes** that involve nested git‑dependent packages; a PAT works for a simple top‑level clone but will be rejected on push inside Ark. Use the SSH key for all write actions.
6. **(Optional) Set your commit identity** so the PR is attributed to you: add `ARK_GIT_AUTHOR_NAME` and `ARK_GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL` at user scope.

After these steps, run your `create_pr` flow again – the push should succeed because Ark will use the stored SSH key with proper permissions.

If you still see an error, double‑check that the secret name matches the workspace exactly and that the key has no passphrase.

A workspace is your project written down once: which repos to clone, which tools to install, which services to run, and which secrets a session needs. ## The CLI way 
Use this if you would rather stay in the terminal. It needs your own personal API key, the same one from [Getting Access](/onboarding/getting-access). It must be an identity-bound user key: a shared key will not work.
**Step 1** \- Search for **Ark-bot** in Slack.
**Step 2 - Mint your link token** (any terminal with the `ark` CLI):
bash
    
    ark slack link \
      --server https://ark.internal.ap-south-1.platform.mlops.pai.mypaytm.com \
      --token <YOUR_ARK_API_KEY>
The token expires in **15 minutes** and works once - do Step 3 immediately.
Do not reach for `--force`
`--force` mints a link token for **another** user and is a tenant-admin action, so on your own account it fails with `permission denied: tenant.admin at tenant scope`. If you cannot DM the bot, send your Slack member ID to an admin instead.
